skill_title: Describe the magnetic field of a current-carrying conductor and solenoid

items.question: What is produced around a wire that carries an electric current?
items.explanation: A current always produces a magnetic field around the conductor.

items.question: What is the shape of the magnetic field around a long straight current-carrying wire?
items.explanation: The field forms concentric circles around a straight current-carrying conductor.
options: A single dot at the centre.

items.question: The right-hand rule for a straight wire uses the thumb to point in the direction of...
items.explanation: Point the right thumb along the conventional current; the curled fingers show the field direction.

items.question: A coil of wire wound into a long cylinder is called a...
items.explanation: A solenoid is a long coil of wire; carrying current it acts like a bar magnet.

items.question: A current-carrying solenoid produces a magnetic field similar to that of a...
items.explanation: A solenoid behaves like a bar magnet, with a north and south pole.

items.question: What happens to the magnetic field direction if the current in a wire is reversed?
items.explanation: Reversing the current reverses the direction of the magnetic field.

items.question: Which change would make an electromagnet (solenoid) stronger?
items.expectedAnswer: Increasing the current or adding more turns.
items.explanation: More current, more turns, or an iron core all strengthen the field.
options: Increasing the current or adding more turns.

items.question: Adding an iron core to a solenoid does what to its magnetic field?
items.explanation: A soft-iron core concentrates and strengthens the magnetic field.

items.question: Further from a straight current-carrying wire, the magnetic field is...
items.explanation: The field weakens with distance from the wire (the circles spread apart).

items.question: An advantage of an electromagnet over a permanent magnet is that...
items.expectedAnswer: it can be switched on and off.
items.explanation: An electromagnet's field can be turned on or off and varied with the current.
options: it can be switched on and off.

items.question: Using the right-hand rule, if conventional current flows upward in a vertical wire, the field on the wire's left side (facing it) points...
items.expectedAnswer: out of the page toward you / around the wire anticlockwise (as seen from above).
items.explanation: Curling the right hand around the upward current gives a circular field; the rule sets its direction around the wire.
options: out of the page toward you / around the wire anticlockwise (as seen from above).
there is no field beside the wire.

items.question: Why does using conventional current (not electron flow) matter for the right-hand rule?
items.expectedAnswer: Conventional current is opposite to electron flow, so using the wrong one reverses the predicted field.
items.explanation: Conventional current flows opposite to electrons; the right-hand rule is defined for conventional current.
options: Conventional current is opposite to electron flow, so using the wrong one reverses the predicted field.

items.question: Two parallel wires carry current in the SAME direction. They tend to...
items.explanation: Parallel currents in the same direction attract (their fields interact).
options: have no effect on each other.

items.question: How can you reverse the poles of a solenoid electromagnet?
items.expectedAnswer: Reverse the direction of the current.
items.explanation: Reversing the current swaps the north and south poles of the solenoid.
options: Reverse the direction of the current.

items.question: Compared with a single straight wire, why is a solenoid's field stronger and more uniform inside?
items.expectedAnswer: The fields of many turns add together inside the coil.
items.explanation: Each turn contributes to the field; inside the solenoid these combine into a strong, fairly uniform field.
options: There is no current in a single wire.
The fields of many turns add together inside the coil.

items.question: An electromagnet is used in a scrapyard crane. Why is an electromagnet better than a permanent magnet here?
items.expectedAnswer: It can be switched on to lift and off to drop the metal.
items.explanation: Switching it off releases the load — impossible with a permanent magnet.
options: It can be switched on to lift and off to drop the metal.
It is always on, which is safer.

items.question: If the number of turns on a solenoid is doubled (same current), the magnetic field strength roughly...
items.explanation: More turns per length increases the field strength of the solenoid.

items.question: The magnetic field lines inside a solenoid point from...
items.expectedAnswer: its south pole to its north pole (inside), completing the loop.
items.explanation: Like a bar magnet, field lines run N→S outside and S→N inside, forming closed loops.
options: its south pole to its north pole (inside), completing the loop.

items.question: What evidence shows that a current-carrying wire has a magnetic field?
items.expectedAnswer: A nearby compass needle deflects when the current flows.
items.explanation: A compass placed near the wire deflects, showing the presence of a magnetic field (Oersted's discovery).
options: A nearby compass needle deflects when the current flows.

items.question: Two parallel wires carry current in OPPOSITE directions. They tend to...
items.explanation: Antiparallel currents repel each other through their magnetic interaction.
